correctness.rationale: For distinct circuit-hyperplanes H,H′ the sparse-paving intersection bound gives x(H)+x(H′)<=2r-2 on the whole hypersimplex, so their excised strict vertex corners are disjoint. A single new facet is the orthogonal product of two standard simplices and has exact (n-2)-area sqrt(r(n-r))/((r-1)!(n-r-1)!). For each removed vertex, exactly r coordinate-one and n-r coordinate-zero original facet caps are lost, each with the computed pyramid volume. The alternating Eulerian formula gives the hypersimplex baseline. Subtracting additive caps and adding complete new facets proves the stated formula. Positivity follows from a>=r(n-r) and c sqrt(r(n-r))>sqrt(2), and the rank-monotonicity comparison follows from the explicitly proved consecutive-rank inequality. The canonical n=6,r=3 example has exact area 4sqrt(5)+3/2. Independent convex-hull computations passed 73 cases and 76 rank profiles.

value.rationale: Sparse-paving matroid polytopes form a large, naturally defined class. Ordinary Euclidean surface area, unlike lattice boundary normalization, is metric and depends on facet normal norms. The theorem gives a complete exact valuation on all connected sparse-paving base polytopes, proving that intersection patterns cannot affect it even though published f-vector formulas are sensitive to those patterns. The rank-balanced maximal loss is a nontrivial sharp inequality for the per-circuit metric defect. The explicitly constructed six-element pair has the same Euclidean area but different face vectors. This is motivated geometric structure, not an arbitrary finite recomputation; it does not claim to classify all intrinsic volumes.
